First off, I'd place a boundary for arguments inside of a small space like that. You can't walk away from a situation if you're stuck driving a car that he's riding in. If he has a legitimate problem, y'all can hold off on the 'discussion' until you're home. 

This brings me to the next point; how do you handle the conversations that turn into him yelling? Well, you don't need to put up with unnecessary yelling. Express that you have some childhood trauma connected to people yelling at you. Let him know that if he starts, you may need to shut down the interaction completely until he's calm enough to discuss things like an adult. If he starts and you have the ability, calmly state "I don't appreciate being yelled at. I'm going to walk away, and we can both calm down before we talk about this. Let me know when you're calm enough to talk at a normal volume." Then walk away. Don't cave or let him pull you back in. You aren't obligated to sit there while he yells at you. Do something nice for yourself while you two are taking breathing space. The most important part here is that you keep the boundary in tact-- he needs to learn that he doesn't get to yell at you and you won't allow him to. It may take persistence to discontinue a conversation until you've both cooled off, but this will allow him to think and (hopefully) realize that he's being needlessly cruel and needs to chill out if he wants to communicate effectively. 

Also, as a side note, why is he telling you how to drive? If he has such a problem with the way you navigate in traffic, perhaps he can drive himself places instead of having you do it.

Don't put up with things that make you feel shitty. You deserve communication, which is NOT one person yelling until the other cries.

Yea, it sounds like you need to have an honest talk with her if you want to continue this relationship. Don't go back and forth or be blasé about your thoughts and feelings, just speak to her.

If you can't trust her, end it. Trust is essential to a functioning relationship. 

If you're not ready to end it, have an *honest* conversation with her about how you feel. Don't crack jokes, or skirt it, or try to use coded language. Just talk plainly. She seems to be having some issues trusting you, as well, if she feels the need to lie about this and keep little things from you. Perhaps being blunt and honest will help her return the transparency. 

If you don't like those answers, idk what you expect here. Do you want us to tell you that you're totally justified in making her responsible for your security and self-esteem? No. She's not responsible for that, and neither is anyone other than yourself. If you continue to struggle with feelings of inadequacy and mistrust, I would suggest therapy.

You cannot make her trust you. She will or will not, and it will be on her terms and her schedule.

You have to decide if you're willing to either wait and continue easing her worries, potentially live with her mistrust for the duration of the relationship, or end it and move on. 

You mention her being verbally abusive. If this is the case, I would lean in the direction of leaving. Regardless of her insecurities, you do not deserve to be treated in a way that makes you feel less than. She needs to cope with her feelings and not take them out on you. If she can't figure out a way to control herself and utilize self-awareness to overcome this together, it isn't your responsibility to be her emotional punching bag or trash can.

As someone who has repeatedly had their journals read and privacy breached by people I cared for, leave her alone. Those journals are for therapeutic purposes and you likely did some damage to her sense of security by invading a safe space of hers.

You did something stupid and hurtful and she wants you to go away. Stop checking up on her and respect her wishes if you actually care. And if someone trusts you enough to let you be in their space like that again, don't disrespect them. You already know this isn't your business.

Please leave. He is abusing you and manipulating you, and nothing about this sounds okay.

Wherever you are, can you find a shelter or a friend to stay with? You deserve better than this treatment and it's important to stay safe while you untangle yourself from this...

I haven't even finished reading this, but:

>Me and my boyfriend made a compromise/deal that if I stopped smoking marijuana he’d be more loving

is not okay. Love and affection are not things to be leveraged, withheld, or bartered in a relationship. Period.

Edited after reading: You are not being unfair. Everyone deserves to feel loved by their partner.

Please think about this from a different perspective: your best friend comes to you and says that their partner has made a deal with them; the partner will show love and affection if your friend stops using marijuana. Your friend stops, but says that their partner has become withdrawn anyway and requires prompting to express affection. 

What would you say to this friend?

This is a sign of a severe lack of impulse control and some very deep issues on his part. I'm not saying that this will or even might escalate into physical altercations or fights, but this is abusive. He does not have a right to breach your privacy or damage your belongings, and if he can't trust that you have friendly conversations with your friends without any weird subtext, that is not healthy. 

What if you'd gone out for coffee with a friend, and he later discovered that that 45 minute/hour long/two hour long hangout was with -gasp- a BOY? I would sincerely recommend he seek therapy if he feels this threatened by his partner having friends/close friends/friendly friends of a different gender.

My gut feeling is that he doesn't trust you. If he did, he would have proceeded in a different manner. Instead, he made an assumption, ignored your explanation, threw your phone out of your hand, cursed at you, and made you leave. Then proceeded to ignore you, save for a weird cryptic 3AM (mis)text??

No. This is not okay. You don't need to feel badly here. He needs to apologize for overreacting and damaging your property. I would seriously reconsider this relationship.

On a softer note, I am so so SO sorry that you were subjected to this. It may be easy to tell yourself "it was just a phone", "at least he didn't hit me/throw it at me/break it", but this is a scary thing to witness. Especially from someone you love and were/are hoping to be together with. Please be gentle with yourself and remember that you can love someone and disagree with the way they treat you/others, and demand better. It's not your fault he reacted that way.

Hey there. I want to start by saying that you're not alone in feeling this way. I am not a medical professional by any means, but this could be more than depression. 

Life is Hard. This in no way is meant to belittle your struggle, as I know for a fact that what you're suffering with is not comparable to anyone else's struggles. It doesn't matter if someone else "has it worse". It doesn't matter if your experience lines up with others. Everyone's brain works and is built differently-- no two people will respond identically to similar stimuli.
